subject: Sparse regression using horseshoe priors and small effects

messages.author: 2d0c12cf9869e063
messages.subject: Sparse regression using horseshoe priors and small effects
parts:
I'm attempting to set up a multivariate sparse regression using the code from Piironen & Vehtari 2015 for a horseshoe prior on the regression coefficients, 
but I think I'm having some problems with over shrinkage of the non-noise components, since they are expected to be small (around 0.1 - 0.2 sd).

So, my question is, how can I modify the priors to take the expected scale of the non-null effects into account?

I currently have: 
transformed parameters{
   
    real<lower=0> tau;
    matrix<lower=0>[K, J] lambda;
    matrix[K, J] w;

    tau = r1_global * sqrt(r2_global);

    lambda = r1_local .* sqrt_vec(r2_local);

    w = beta .* lambda * tau;
}

and in the model section:

           for (n in 1:N)
              mu[n] = w0 + w * ad[n] + beta_family[family[n]];
 to_vector(beta) ~ normal(0, 1);
 to_vector(r1_local) ~ normal(0.0, 1.0);
 to_vector(r2_local) ~ inv_gamma(0.5, 0.5);

 // half cauchy for tau
 r1_global ~ normal(0.0, 1.0);
 r2_global ~ inv_gamma(0.5, 0.5);


Full model is attached, any input is much appreciated! 

Thanks,

Diogo Melo

messages.author: fc5d3270037d7478
messages.subject: Sparse regression using horseshoe priors and small effects
parts:
I think the hierarchical shrinkage (and hierarchical shrinkage plus) priors they describe in

http://arxiv.org/abs/1508.02502

are preferable to the horseshoe. Essentially the same thing but with a t distribution with df > 1 (so shorter tail than the Cauchy) rather than the horseshoe.

When I've fit the horseshoe in the past I've also always had to set a small initial stepsize and increase adapt_delta (the target acceptance rate).

And I second Bob's recommendation to check with simulated data if you haven't already.

Jonah

On Wed, Jul 13, 2016 at 6:16 AM, Jonah Gabry <jga...@gmail.com> wrote:
I think the hierarchical shrinkage (and hierarchical shrinkage plus) priors they describe in

http://arxiv.org/abs/1508.02502

are preferable to the horseshoe. Essentially the same thing but with a t distribution with df > 1 (so shorter tail than the Cauchy) rather than the horseshoe.

I've based my model on this paper, but saw little difference from using 1 or 3 dfs, and don't have the problem of excessive divergent transitions using the 1 df. 
I think since I'm getting excessive shrinkage using the shorter tails would be a bad idea, right?
When I've fit the horseshoe in the past I've also always had to set a small initial stepsize and increase adapt_delta (the target acceptance rate).

Using simulated data with large effects the convergence seems ok, and it's running in reasonable time. I do get the occasional warning on setting adapt_delta above 0.8.
Can this cause a problem with the model fit?

thanks!

d.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Sparse regression using horseshoe priors and small effects
parts:
> On Jul 13, 2016, at 5:34 AM, Diogo Melo <dio...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> ...

> Using simulated data with large effects the convergence seems ok, and it's running in reasonable time. I do get the occasional warning on setting adapt_delta above 0.8.
> Can this cause a problem with the model fit?

Yes, divergent transitions can cause bias if they
occur non-randomly.

And if models are poorly specified with respect to the data,
they can be hard to fit, too.

- Bob

messages.author: 2d0c12cf9869e063
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Sparse regression using horseshoe priors and small effects
parts:
Okay, I'm convinced.

Changing to a Horseshoe+ prior and using larger degrees of freedom the divergent transitions all but disappear.
The estimates look very similar. 

One rather hackish solution that produces better results was to re-scale the traits to much higher variance (from 1 to 20 or 30).
This puts the coefficients on the unit scale and the shrinkage problem is somewhat reduced.

Are there any disadvantages on doing this? Currently the variance parameters have a Cauchy(0, 2.5) prior.

messages.author: a236d3d356ca53fd
messages.subject: Re: Sparse regression using horseshoe priors and small effects
parts:
- It's usually a good idea to scale all the covariates to have unit variance
- degrees of freedom in hierarchical shrinkage prior controls on proprty of the shape of the shrinkage curve, if the degrees of freedom is nu=1 then small number of effects should not be shrunk at all and you don't need to know the expected scale, but you need to know the expected number of non-zero effects
- any of the scale parameters of the normals in the prior can be used to set the width of the prior (e.g. the normal prior for the beta). The width will affect the assumption about the number of the non-zero effects. Unfortunately I don't have yet a good recommendation how to choose this, but you can easily experiment with your own data,

Aki
